fr:title.text: JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization
fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @misc{tschandJAXBenchBenchmarkingAutonomous2026, title = {{{JAXBench}}: {{Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization}}}, author = {Tschand, Arya and Hong, Charles and Walker, Julian and Cai, Nina and Wang, Shangkun and Subramanian, Suvinay and Dev, Sundar and Reddi, Vijay Janapa and Yazdanbakhsh, Amir and Sankaran, Sethu}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2607.20466}, urldate = {2026-08-03}, number = {arXiv:2607.20466}, publisher = {arXiv}, file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/JAXBench Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization - Tschand et al..pdf}, keywords = {Computer Science - Artificial Intelligence}, langid = {english}, archiveprefix = {arXiv}, abstract = {Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8\% to 37.3\% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.}, primaryclass = {cs.AI}, eprint = {2607.20466}, month = {May}, shorttitle = {{{JAXBench}}} }

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another week another weekly review! One of the few things I am at least doing consistently now. For all those that I am missing, I refer you to this weeks entry of life maxing. On another note, I am one with the TPU. My heart rate is no longer 48bpm but instead 6 bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] matmuls per minuteThis is an MXU reference. Also running is not good for my clock speed....

I have spent SO much time on my computer this week. My eyes are in a perpetual state of bloodshotIf somehow someone reading this has good eyedrops or some other remedy PLEASE reach out. This ultrawide monitor seemed like a good idea until one actually spends ~10hrs a day staring at it.

An eternity was spent on this forest. A good portion of this has been toward finally sitting down and getting a grip on TPUs via How to scale your model. I have actually made decent progress on the exercises and the corresponding notebook.
Unfortunately, the accompanying beautiful animations found in ReduceScatter and Systolic array were a less productive but equally tracked usage of my time.

The tokamax time is a bit of a hint to what I am cooking up. Due to the likely scenario no one is reading this, there will be an accompanying blog I am also working on Bringing Speed-of-Light FlexAttention to TPU. If {people working on this} \cap {people reading this} \neq \emptyset . Then email me and we can combine forces!
I mean these numbers speak for themselves. 50hrs actively on a computer are enough to make the terminators' eye blood vessels detonate. Luckily only my eyes and not my brain are rotting.

Yeah I take creatine guysand you should too.. Outside of that, I am a bit of a bum. I reduced my stretch routine to a mere 23min and that actually has allowed me to pick my consistency back up. Leetcode is a more of an active choice than laziness. I have grown bearish on the value of the exercise and if I want to throw my name in the DSA rat race. I think my time is better spent on anything TPU or GPU related.

In addition to my general computer science cards, I have begun to make a deck for the scaling book. This is the first time I have been actively reviewing cards as I progress through a book, and it makes a world of a difference. Will definitely be doing this for the next book.

I am but a humble nomad in my long journey toward TPU sensei-ship. Unfortunately (or fortunately?), I am still firmly on the left end of the Dunning-Kruger curve. I am progressing slowly but very dilligently through the How to scale your model. I want to be on chapter 5 by end of next week. The remaining chapter 3 exercises seem like they may take awhile and chapter 4 is equally important as it is dense, so I want to make sure I give it a proper treatment. An additional mini reading / todo list:

html:ul.html:li: CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution - seems interesting but the paper is kind of bare bones on first pass.
Want to be able to read the whole TPU pipeline. This primarily means setting up the TPU infrastructure but also a good set of blogs here, here, and here.
Need to come up with definitive proposal for project.
Importantly, why non-agentic approaches cannot compete in JaxBench-regime.
Maybe walk through how each method does GQA?
Be able to defend choice of TPU.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As a bit of a productivity aside, I have noticed that I am wasting a lot of my prime deep work bandwidth in the morning on the transfer / organization of notes into this forest during reading. Additionally, my post-lunch block is very ineffective. I had the genius idea of eliminating the cognitive overhead of organizing and transferring notes by deferring until the afternoon block. In the morning block, I will just dump everything I might care about later. Then, in the later block, I will do the menial, low cognitive demand task of choosing what stays and where it goes. This can also serve as a form of review.

Furthermore, I have officially setup a technology free desk to take this to the extreme. This will hopefully serve as my paper reading station or when I am rich enough to get physical textbooks. I have an accompanying notebook to write down any questions I need to ask Claude after the pomo block ends, or write down relevant notes to transfer later. I have consistently avoided doing this because I believe quickly asking Claude is a necessity. However, I hope to find that writing down and thinking about questions independently first will not be that bad and may even be useful.
